items_missed: Never asked how the customer was, and never confirmed his name. Joel has 'Sonny' from the lead record and uses it twice late in the call, but he never asked for or verified it at the open.

The move date was never asked. This is the strangest gap in an otherwise thorough call — Joel probed the garage, both patios, the antique curio, the glass cabinets and the box count, and never once asked when the customer needs to move. Dates only enter the conversation when Joel proposes 'October 4th' out of nowhere late in the call, which sets off a three-minute muddle: the customer says 'Sunday would be great actually, the twenty sixth,' Joel corrects him to the twenty seventh, the customer then says he will be out of town, and they eventually land on Friday October 2. That entire detour is what asking 'when are you looking to move?' at minute one prevents.

The agenda statement was there in substance — 'I can just ask you a few additional questions just to kind of get a better idea of what we'll be moving and then we can kind of go from there... for any move that's larger than $1,800 we would like to get a virtual walkthrough completed' — but it never got a confirmation ask attached to it. No 'sound good?', no 'does that work for you?' tied to the roadmap, so the agenda_opener flag does not fire.

Special considerations never probed — no long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns, on a move between two three-story townhomes. Stairwell turns are the single most common reason a three-story job runs over, and neither end was asked about.
Access concerns never probed — no parking, no driveway, no gate or HOA question at either townhome.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, and the customer telegraphed his stressor in the first ninety seconds: he wants to shed roughly forty percent of his furniture and does not know how. 'I want to get rid of some of my furniture. Is it possible for you to move sixty percent of my stuff... can you bring the stuff that I don't want to the dump?' Joel answered the logistics correctly and never engaged with the worry underneath it.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. Not once, across twenty-one minutes, on a 3,400 square foot home containing an antique case, glass-front cabinets, a curio 'that has mostly glass and a lot of knickknacks in it,' and an oak dining table, moving down and up three flights of stairs. This is the biggest content miss on the call.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — and it would have fit naturally, because Joel voluntarily walked through the entire pre-move communication cadence ('we'll send you a courtesy text like a few days prior to the move... we'll send another text the day before'). Meet Your Mover is exactly the email that belongs in that sequence and he described the sequence without it.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned, despite Joel committing to a specific arrival window ('plan for them to arrive about 8:30 ish').

No sense-check in the clock explanation, and the cost of that is visible in the transcript. Immediately after the clock section the customer interrupted, confused: 'why are you charging by the hour, why are you giving me an estimate, I guess the estimate is just an estimate, right? Is that what you're telling me?' A four-second 'does that make sense?' after the two-and-a-half-hour minimum would have caught that before it became a customer-initiated challenge to the whole quote.

Stairs were never factored into the estimate. The customer himself pointed out the structure — 'so you're going from a three story to the other three story' — and Joel's reply was 'Here. Okay, that's pretty much everything that I needed.' Six and a half to eight and a half hours is a generic 3,400 square foot number; nothing in it accounts for two three-story properties.
Truck count never stated. Four movers were specified precisely and repeatedly; the customer never learned how many trucks that is.
Walk distance never asked at either end, and no equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make seven to eight hours concrete.

No email handoff of any kind. Joel described the text cadence in detail and never once said he would send a confirmation email — no email address collected, no bolded details, no 'reply with any corrections.' The customer booked a Friday October 2 move, a Tuesday 11 AM virtual walkthrough, and a four-mover crew, and has nothing in writing. On a $2,800 to $3,200 job with a separate walkthrough appointment attached, that is the most consequential process gap on the call.
Hours and how-to-reach-us never given. The customer knows Joel will call him; he has no number and no window to call in.

The discount explanation fell apart under a direct question and never fully recovered. The customer asked 'you're talking about $200 per hour?' and got 'No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no, not the hourly rate. The hourly rate is about, I'd say about $1,624 cheaper, but $24 times eight that's where you get that $200 just about $200.' The underlying math is right — $408 versus $384 an hour, $24 an hour across eight hours — but it arrived as a jumble, and the customer disengaged from the discount entirely right afterwards ('I don't care about $200').
Customer's name used twice, short of the 3+ standard, and both uses are in the same closing stretch.
top_strength: Joel delivered the only genuine Save Your Ass speech in this week's sample, and he did it unprompted, at the right moment, and tied directly to the estimate he had just given. Right after quoting seven to eight hours and $2,800 to $3,200, he volunteered the lever: 'I think one thing that could make it less if by chance like you said you're moving a lot of the boxes yourself, maybe some of the smaller things too, basically all the small things that you can get moved over, the quicker the move should go. The moving team's very efficient with all the big furniture and boxes. Where they lose a little bit more time, it's the little things that need to be moved like the lamps, kitchen appliances, portraits, things like that. Those require a little bit more packing and prepping by our team. So that's where a little bit more time gets lost. It's just protecting those items from scratches and scuffs. It's the little things, but if you're able to get that moved over, then that should save a little bit more time and make sure that we stay on track with the estimate.' That is the whole speech: prep equals a shorter move equals a lower bill, with real consolidation examples, tied to the customer's own stated plan to carry boxes over himself on a five-minute drive, and closed with the accuracy argument rather than just the savings argument. He followed it with 'Any questions there regarding that quote?' Across 267 cumulative graded calls, Save Your Ass has landed only 19 times — this is a clip worth pulling for the calibration session. The probing behind it was equally strong. Joel asked about the garage and then caught that there were two patios, not one, and scoped both separately: 'anything in the patio that needs to be moved by us?' → 'Oh, oh, I have two patios' → 'One has a desk and two chairs and two chairs. And then one has two chairs and the cat stand.' He then ran a clean specialty-items sweep — heavy items, glass and marble and stone, appliances, workout equipment, antique furniture, large book collections — and gave the box count an anchor before asking for it rather than after: 'how many boxes do you expect to have? Just a general idea, we typically see about 110 to 140, do you think that sounds about right?' which let the customer correct it down to fifty with confidence. His rate framing was the most correct in the sample — '$408 an hour for a four man crew, so it's $102 per mover per hour' — with the full inclusion list right behind it: 'the gas, taxes, insurance, our truck, all the moving blankets, the shrink wrap bands, everything needed to protect your furniture in the home. Also all the tools for any assembly, disassembly.' And the clock section is textbook: 'our time won't begin until we arrive there on site, we'll go ahead and sign the contract with you. Our time will begin, our moving team will then do a quick walkthrough just to be sure that everything is on par with the estimate. We do have a two and a half hour minimum. And then after our minimum is met we go up in increments of fifteen minutes.' He also handled the one thing he could not do — the dump run — without losing the customer, giving a clean no and a real alternative ('we would need you to probably hire like a junk removal company'), then circled back later to help him sequence it: 'maybe you can do the junk hauling on that day and get the junk removal to show up on that day.' Finally, he set the walkthrough expectation honestly rather than overselling the phone quote: 'right now it'll be kind of a ballpark figure of what we typically see. But once I do that virtual walkthrough with you that's where I'll be able to give you a more accurate quote.'
coaching_note: Classified as walkthrough_scheduler because Joel opened by routing this 3,400 square foot job to a virtual walkthrough on the stated $1,800 threshold and booked it for Tuesday at 11 AM — so on a strict reading, the pricing, clock, estimate and Save Your Ass sections do not cleanly apply to this call type and the pending mini-rubric would score it on Set Agenda, Probe, Walkthrough booking and Politeness only. That said, Joel ran the full sales motion anyway and booked the actual move on the same call, so those sections have been graded against the 85-point rubric on their merits rather than waived — the score should be read with that caveat, not compared straight across to a pure intake call. Highest-leverage fix, and it is not a small one: there is no email. Joel booked a Friday October 2 move with a four-mover crew, a Tuesday 11 AM virtual walkthrough, and a $2,800 to $3,200 estimate, and the customer has nothing in writing — no confirmation, no email address collected, no bolded details, no reply-with-corrections ask. He substituted the text cadence for it ('we'll send you a courtesy text like a few days prior'), which is a reminder system, not a record. For a customer who spent the call correcting himself on dates, misremembering the twenty-sixth versus the twenty-seventh, and asking twice how the discount math worked, the written confirmation is the thing that prevents a no-show or a day-of dispute. Add it to the close, every call: 'I'm sending a confirmation email right now with the date, the crew, the rate and the estimate bolded at the top — give it a read and reply with any corrections so I know I've got it right.' Second priority: ask for the move date in the first two minutes. Not asking it is what produced the three-minute date scramble at the end of a twenty-one-minute call, and it is also why Joel found himself proposing dates rather than filling a date the customer already had in mind. Third, name No Worries Damage Coverage. A 3,400 square foot home with an antique case, glass-front cabinets and a knickknack-filled curio going down three flights and up three more is the highest damage-risk job in this week's sample, and the coverage was never mentioned. 'Every move includes No Worries Damage Coverage — up to $2,000 to repair, replace or reimburse accidental damage, already in the rate. Most movers cover sixty cents a pound' is thirty seconds and it is the reassurance this specific inventory calls for. Estimate-accuracy note, and this one is a credit rather than a flag: Joel did not pad. He stated the typical range as six and a half to eight and a half hours, landed 'right in the middle, seven to eight,' priced both ends, and explicitly declined to pretend the phone number was final — 'once I do that virtual walkthrough that's where I'll be able to give you a more accurate quote.' That is the correct discipline and it is the opposite of the conservative-padding pattern driving the 46 percent number. The one real accuracy gap is stairs: two three-story townhomes and not a minute of the estimate is attributable to them, even after the customer pointed the structure out himself. Worth carrying into the Tuesday walkthrough as the specific thing to measure, and worth pulling the actual against the seven-to-eight-hour booking when the job runs. One last coaching point on delivery: the discount explanation ('the hourly rate is about, I'd say about $1,624 cheaper, but $24 times eight') lost the customer completely, and he waved off a real $200 saving because he could not follow it. The clean version is 'Sunday is $384 an hour instead of $408 — that's $24 an hour, so across an eight-hour day it's about $200 off the total.'
phone_presence_notes: Consistently respectful and unhurried with a customer who wandered, repeated himself and changed his mind on dates three times — steady 'Yes sir,' 'Cool,' 'Awesome,' patient re-explanations when asked the same question twice, a graceful no on the dump request that came with a real alternative, and a genuinely helpful unprompted money-saving tip; held at 4 rather than 5 by no warm-up question at the open, his name used only twice, and a garbled discount explanation that left the customer more confused than when he asked.
audio_review_reason: The efficiency bullet was deducted partly on the discount exchange, and the transcript there is unreliable enough that it cannot carry the deduction on its own — 'The hourly rate is about, I'd say about $1,624 cheaper, but $24 times eight that's where you get that $200' is either a rep genuinely fumbling the math out loud or a transcription mangling of a clean '$16 to $24 cheaper' style sentence. The date sequence has the same problem ('September 27th is a Sunday not the twenty sixth twenty seventh' followed by 'Well he'll forget to twenty seventh that work'). Audio would settle whether the confusion in this call is Joel's delivery or the transcript's, which matters because he is otherwise one of the cleanest scripts in the sample.
